“The SuperB Silicon Vertex Detector (SVT) is the largest CMOS MAPS experiment ever built, with a total active area of about 1 m 2 and a total of more than 1.3 billion pixels.

we have successfully demonstrated that: 1) the INMAPS and the Tezzaron 3 D CMOS processes can produce thin MAPS sensors with performances comparable to those obtained with the ST Microelectronics DNW process and with the same functionalities; 2) the INMAPs process allows to implement a more efficient in-pixel charge collection and 3) the 3D process allows to develop a faster in-pixel readout.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of CMOS MAPS with a pixel size of 50 μm x 50 μ m, a thickness of about 100 μ m and an active area of about 10 cm 2.
the development of CMOS MAPS with improved charge collection efficiency and faster readout, in order to meet the challenging SuperB requirements.
the development of CMOS MAPS with a view to the SuperB experiment, with a special emphasis on the realization of a fast readout architecture.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CMOS MAPS technology has now reached a level of maturity which makes it a very promising candidate for the realization of the SuperB Layer 0.
the SuperB project is a unique opportunity for the development of innovative CMOS sensors, which will be the basis for the future generation of pixel detectors in high energy physics experiments.
the MAPS technology is now mature enough to be considered for the realization of a large area silicon pixel detector.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the INMAPS process has been successfully applied to produce a MAPS sensor prototype, with a pixel size of 25  μ m  ×  25  μ m, featuring the same basic functionalities as the standard DNW MAPs.
we have demonstrated that MAPS can be successfully used for tracking applications at high luminosity and that the technology is mature enough to be used in a collider experiment.

, thanks to the R&D efforts in the past few years, CMOS MAPS technology is now mature enough to be considered as a viable alternative to the hybrid solution in view of the construction of future vertex detectors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CMOS technology, in the form of thin MAPS, is a very promising option for the SuperB Layer-0.
CMOS MAPS technology is now a valid alternative to the hybrid technology for the implementation of a high resolution pixel detector.

3D and quadruple-well CMOS processes can be used to improve the performance of MAPS, and in particular the 3D technology can provide an interesting solution to the problem of high background hit rates.
